stem: Which component of blood transports oxygen?

options.rationale: Their haemoglobin combines with oxygen.
White blood cells defend the body against pathogens.
Platelets help blood to clot.
A little oxygen dissolves in plasma, but almost all is carried by haemoglobin in red blood cells.

explanation: Red blood cells contain haemoglobin, which combines with oxygen in the lungs and releases it in the tissues.
hints: Which cells contain haemoglobin?

stem: Which component of blood helps it to clot?

options.rationale: Red cells are trapped in a clot but do not start clotting.
Lymphocytes make antibodies.
Platelets collect at a wound and help start the clotting process.
Water is the solvent of plasma; it does not cause clotting.

explanation: Platelets are cell fragments that collect at a damaged blood vessel and help to start the reactions that form a clot.
hints: They are tiny fragments of cells.

stem: True or false: human red blood cells have no nucleus.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Correct. Without a nucleus there is more room for haemoglobin.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: It is true. Mature red blood cells lose their nucleus, leaving more room for haemoglobin.

explanation: Mature human red blood cells have no nucleus, so there is more space for haemoglobin and each cell can carry more oxygen.
hints: What fills almost all the space inside a red blood cell?

stem: Which substance is carried **dissolved in the plasma**?

options.rationale: Haemoglobin is inside the red blood cells.

options.content: Oxygen, which is carried mainly in the plasma
options.rationale: Most oxygen is carried by haemoglobin in red blood cells, not dissolved in plasma.
Phagocytes are cells carried in the blood, not dissolved substances.
Urea from the liver dissolves in the plasma and is carried to the kidneys.

explanation: Plasma carries dissolved substances such as urea, glucose, amino acids, mineral ions, hormones and carbon dioxide. Oxygen is carried mainly by haemoglobin inside red blood cells.
hints: Which substance is made in the liver and removed by the kidneys?

stem: Name the red pigment in red blood cells that combines with oxygen.

rejected.feedback: Iron is part of the pigment, but the pigment itself is haemoglobin.
Chlorophyll is the green pigment in plants.
Plasma is the liquid part of blood.

explanation: Haemoglobin is an iron-containing protein. In the lungs it combines with oxygen to form oxyhaemoglobin; in the tissues it releases the oxygen.
hints: It contains iron.

stem: Match each component of blood with its function.

right.content: Transport dissolved substances such as glucose, urea and hormones

explanation: Red cells carry oxygen; white cells defend against pathogens; platelets help clotting; plasma carries dissolved substances. Bile is made by the liver.
hints: One function belongs to an organ, not to blood.

stem: How does having no nucleus help a red blood cell to do its job?

options.content: It lets the cell divide faster.
options.rationale: Without a nucleus, red blood cells cannot divide at all.

options.content: It leaves more room for haemoglobin, so the cell can carry more oxygen.
options.rationale: More haemoglobin means more oxygen carried.

options.content: It lets the cell make antibodies.
options.rationale: Antibodies are made by lymphocytes.

options.content: It makes the cell heavier, so it sinks out of the blood into the tissues.
options.rationale: Red cells stay in the blood vessels.

explanation: A red blood cell without a nucleus has more space for haemoglobin, so each cell can carry more oxygen.
hints: What fills the space a nucleus would have taken?

stem: Red blood cells are biconcave discs. How does this shape help them?

options.content: It lets them wrap around and engulf bacteria in the blood.
options.rationale: Phagocytes engulf bacteria.

options.content: It stops them passing through capillaries.
options.rationale: They must pass through capillaries; their flexible shape helps.

options.content: It gives a large surface area, so oxygen diffuses in and out quickly.
options.rationale: The biconcave shape increases the surface area and shortens the distance to the centre.

options.content: It makes room for a large nucleus that controls haemoglobin production.
options.rationale: Red blood cells have no nucleus.

explanation: The biconcave shape gives a large surface area compared with the volume of the cell and a short distance to its centre, so oxygen diffuses in and out quickly.
hints: Think about surface area and diffusion.

stem: (Supplement) Which type of white blood cell makes antibodies?

options.rationale: Phagocytes engulf and digest pathogens.
Lymphocytes make antibodies that attach to particular pathogens.
Platelets are cell fragments involved in clotting.
Red cells carry oxygen.

explanation: Lymphocytes, which have a large round nucleus, make antibodies. Phagocytes, with lobed nuclei, carry out phagocytosis.
hints: It has a large, round nucleus.

stem: (Supplement) In a photomicrograph of blood, a cell larger than the red cells has a nucleus divided into several lobes. Bacteria can be seen inside it. What is this cell, and what is it doing?

options.rationale: Lymphocytes have a large round nucleus, and they do not engulf bacteria.

options.content: A red blood cell carrying oxygen to cells
options.rationale: Red blood cells have no nucleus.
Platelets are tiny fragments with no nucleus.
A lobed nucleus and engulfed bacteria identify a phagocyte.

explanation: A large cell with a lobed nucleus is a phagocyte. Bacteria inside it have been engulfed and will be digested: phagocytosis.
hints: Which white blood cell has a lobed nucleus?

stem: (Supplement) What happens to fibrinogen when blood clots?

options.content: It is converted into insoluble fibrin, which forms a mesh of threads.
options.rationale: The fibrin mesh traps red blood cells to form a clot.

options.content: It is converted into haemoglobin to replace that lost in bleeding.
options.rationale: Haemoglobin is made in developing red cells and is not involved in clotting.

options.content: It engulfs bacteria at the wound.
options.rationale: Phagocytes engulf bacteria; fibrinogen is a plasma protein.

options.content: It dissolves the clot and its threads once the wound has healed.
options.rationale: Fibrinogen forms the clot; it does not dissolve it.

explanation: At a wound, a chain of reactions started by platelets and damaged tissue converts the soluble plasma protein fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin. The fibrin threads form a mesh that traps red blood cells, forming a clot.
hints: Soluble fibrinogen becomes insoluble ...

stem: True or false: blood clotting helps to stop pathogens entering the body through a wound.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Correct. A clot seals the wound, stopping blood loss and keeping pathogens out.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: It is true. As well as stopping blood loss, a clot seals the wound so pathogens cannot get in.

explanation: Clotting seals a damaged blood vessel. This stops blood loss and forms a barrier, so pathogens cannot enter through the wound.
hints: What could get in through an open wound?

stem: (Supplement) Complete the sentences about blood clotting.

payload.template: At a wound, the soluble plasma protein {{blank:fgn}} is converted into insoluble {{blank:fib}}. This forms a mesh of threads that traps {{blank:rbc}}, forming a clot.

explanation: Fibrinogen (soluble) is converted into fibrin (insoluble). The fibrin threads form a mesh that traps red blood cells, forming the clot.
hints: The soluble form has the longer name.

stem: In a photomicrograph magnified ×1500, a red blood cell measures 12 mm across. Calculate the actual diameter of the cell in micrometres (μm).
explanation: $12\ \text{mm} = 12\,000\ \mu\text{m}$. Actual size $= \dfrac{12\,000}{1500} = 8\ \mu\text{m}$.
workedSolution:
1. Convert to micrometres: $12 \times 1000 = 12\,000\ \mu\text{m}$.
2. Actual size $= \dfrac{\text{image size}}{\text{magnification}} = \dfrac{12\,000}{1500} = 8\ \mu\text{m}$.
hints: Actual size = image size ÷ magnification.

stem: A blood sample contains 4 800 000 red blood cells and 6000 white blood cells per mm³. How many red blood cells are there for each white blood cell?

payload.unitHint: red cells for each white cell

explanation: $\dfrac{4\,800\,000}{6000} = 800$, so there are 800 red blood cells for every white blood cell.
workedSolution: 1. Divide the number of red cells by the number of white cells: $\dfrac{4\,800\,000}{6000} = 800$.
hints: Divide the larger number by the smaller.

stem:
A photomicrograph of a stained blood smear shows four kinds of structure.

| Label | Description |
| --- | --- |
| A | Very many small round cells, paler in the centre, with no nucleus |
| B | A few large cells, each with a dark nucleus divided into several lobes |
| C | A few cells slightly larger than A, each almost filled by one large round nucleus |
| D | Tiny specks, much smaller than A |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Identify A, B, C and D.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Which labelled structure engulfs and digests bacteria?

options.rationale: Red blood cells carry oxygen.
Phagocytes carry out phagocytosis.
Lymphocytes make antibodies.
Platelets help blood to clot.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: A person has far fewer cells of type A than normal. Suggest why this person feels tired and becomes breathless easily.

points.description: Less haemoglobin / fewer red cells, so less oxygen is carried to the tissues
So less aerobic respiration / less energy released in the muscles; breathing becomes faster to try to get more oxygen

parts.explanation: With fewer red blood cells there is less haemoglobin, so less oxygen reaches the tissues. The muscles release less energy by aerobic respiration, so the person feels tired, and breathes faster to try to take in more oxygen.

explanation: A are red blood cells (no nucleus), B phagocytes (lobed nucleus), C lymphocytes (large round nucleus) and D platelets. Phagocytes engulf bacteria. Too few red cells (anaemia) means less oxygen is carried, so less energy is released by respiration.
hints: Use the nucleus to tell the cells apart.
What do red blood cells carry?

stem:
The table shows the results of blood tests on three patients, with the normal ranges used by one laboratory.

| Measurement | Normal range | Patient X | Patient Y | Patient Z |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Haemoglobin / g per 100 cm³ | 12–17 | 8 | 14 | 13 |
| White blood cells / per mm³ | 4000–11 000 | 7000 | 18 000 | 6500 |
| Platelets / per mm³ | 150 000–400 000 | 250 000 | 300 000 | 40 000 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Which patient is most likely to be fighting an infection?

options.rationale: X has a normal white cell count.
Y has a very high white blood cell count.
Z has a normal white cell count.
One white cell count is well above the normal range.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Which patient is most likely to bruise and bleed easily?

options.rationale: X's platelet count is normal.
Y's platelet count is normal.
Z has far fewer platelets than normal, so the blood clots poorly.
Only one patient has a low platelet count.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Patient X feels tired all the time. Suggest a cause of X's result and explain the tiredness.

points.description: Anaemia: low haemoglobin, e.g. from lack of iron in the diet / blood loss / malaria
Less oxygen carried to the cells, so less aerobic respiration / less energy released

parts.explanation: X has anaemia: the haemoglobin level is below normal, perhaps because of a lack of iron in the diet, blood loss or malaria. Less oxygen is carried to the cells, so they release less energy by aerobic respiration and X feels tired.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain why a high white blood cell count suggests an infection.

points.description: White blood cells defend the body against pathogens
More are produced when pathogens are present (to engulf them / make antibodies)

parts.explanation: White blood cells defend the body: phagocytes engulf pathogens and lymphocytes make antibodies. When pathogens invade, the body makes more of them, so the count rises.

explanation: Y's high white cell count suggests an infection; Z's low platelet count means poor clotting; X's low haemoglobin (anaemia) means less oxygen is carried, causing tiredness.
hints: Compare each patient's value with the normal range.
Which component is involved in clotting?

stem: (Supplement) Describe how blood clots when a small blood vessel in the skin is cut, and explain why clotting is important. [5]

points.description: Platelets collect at the wound / damaged tissue and platelets start a chain of reactions
Soluble fibrinogen (a plasma protein) is converted into insoluble fibrin
Fibrin forms a mesh of threads across the wound
The mesh traps red blood cells, forming a clot (which dries to a scab)
Clotting stops (further) blood loss
Clotting stops pathogens entering the body

answerSpec.modelAnswer: When the vessel is cut, platelets collect at the wound and, with the damaged tissue, start a chain of reactions. These convert the soluble plasma protein fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin. The fibrin forms a mesh of threads across the wound that traps red blood cells, forming a clot, which later dries into a scab. Clotting is important because it stops further blood loss and seals the wound so that pathogens cannot enter the body.

explanation: Platelets start the process; fibrinogen becomes fibrin; the fibrin mesh traps red cells. A clot prevents blood loss and keeps pathogens out.
hints: Start with platelets and end with the clot.
Give two reasons why clotting matters.

stem: In which part of the blood is most carbon dioxide transported from the tissues to the lungs?

options.content: In the red blood cells, attached to haemoglobin
options.rationale: Haemoglobin carries oxygen; a little carbon dioxide travels this way, but most is in the plasma.
White blood cells defend the body; they do not transport carbon dioxide.
Platelets are involved in clotting.

options.content: In the plasma, mainly as hydrogencarbonate ions
options.rationale: Most carbon dioxide is carried dissolved in the plasma.

explanation: Carbon dioxide produced by respiring cells is carried to the lungs mainly in the plasma, as hydrogencarbonate ions. Red blood cells carry oxygen.
hints: Plasma carries many dissolved substances, including wastes.

stem: Rudo has anaemia caused by a lack of iron. She becomes breathless and tired much sooner than her friends when they play netball. What is the best explanation?

options.content: Her blood has less haemoglobin, so less oxygen reaches her muscles.
options.rationale: Iron is needed to make haemoglobin.

options.content: Her blood cannot clot, so she loses blood when she runs.
options.rationale: Anaemia does not stop blood clotting.

options.content: She has too few white blood cells, so she catches infections.
options.rationale: Anaemia is about haemoglobin, not white cells.

options.content: Iron gives energy, and she has none to spare.
options.rationale: Iron provides no energy; it is needed to make haemoglobin.

explanation: Iron is needed to make haemoglobin. With less haemoglobin, Rudo's blood carries less oxygen, so her muscles cannot respire aerobically as fast during exercise; she tires sooner and breathes faster to try to get more oxygen.
hints: What is iron used to make?

stem: Select **all** the substances that are transported dissolved in the plasma.

options.rationale: Haemoglobin is inside the red blood cells.
Most carbon dioxide travels in the plasma as hydrogencarbonate ions.
Phagocytes are whole cells carried along in the blood, not substances dissolved in the plasma.
Starch is digested to sugars before absorption, so it does not reach the blood.
Urea is carried in the plasma to the kidneys.
Hormones travel in the plasma to their target organs.
Absorbed glucose is carried in the plasma.

explanation: Plasma carries dissolved glucose, amino acids, mineral ions, urea, hormones and carbon dioxide (as hydrogencarbonate). Haemoglobin is inside red blood cells, and starch must be digested before it can be absorbed.
hints: Three of the options are never dissolved in the plasma.

stem: Some runners spend several weeks training high in the Eastern Highlands, where each breath of air contains less oxygen than at lower altitudes. After a few weeks their blood contains more red blood cells than before. Suggest how this change could help them to run faster when they return to compete at a lower altitude. [4]

points.description: More red blood cells means more haemoglobin
so more oxygen can be carried by each volume of blood / to the muscles
so the muscles can respire aerobically faster, releasing more energy
so less anaerobic respiration / less lactic acid / fatigue is delayed

answerSpec.modelAnswer: With more red blood cells, the runners' blood contains more haemoglobin, so each volume of blood can carry more oxygen from the lungs to the muscles. Back at lower altitude, where the air contains more oxygen, the muscles receive more oxygen per minute, so they can respire aerobically faster and release more energy. Less of the energy has to come from anaerobic respiration, so less lactic acid builds up and fatigue is delayed.

explanation: Extra red blood cells mean extra haemoglobin and more oxygen carried to the muscles, allowing faster aerobic respiration and less reliance on anaerobic respiration.
hints: What do red blood cells contain, and what does it carry?
Link oxygen supply to respiration in the muscles.

stem:
Tatenda had a bacterial throat infection. His white blood cell count was measured every two days.

| Day | 0 | 2 | 4 | 6 | 8 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| White blood cells / per mm³ | 7000 | 15 000 | 18 000 | 11 000 | 7500 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage increase in his white blood cell count between day 0 and day 4. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Describe how his white blood cell count changed over the eight days.

points.description: It rose from 7000 to a peak of 18 000 per mm³ on day 4
then fell back to about the starting value (7500 per mm³) by day 8

parts.explanation: His white cell count rose steeply from 7000 to a peak of 18 000 per mm³ on day 4, then fell back to 7500 per mm³ by day 8, close to its starting value.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: (Supplement) Explain how two types of white blood cell helped him to recover.

points.description: Phagocytes engulf bacteria
and digest them (phagocytosis)
Lymphocytes make antibodies
Antibodies attach to the bacteria / help to destroy them

parts.explanation: Phagocytes moved to the infection and engulfed and digested the bacteria (phagocytosis). Lymphocytes made antibodies, which attached to the bacteria and helped to destroy them.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: What is the most likely reason the count fell after day 4?

options.content: The infection was being cleared, so fewer white blood cells were needed.
options.rationale: As the bacteria were destroyed, the extra white cells were no longer made.

options.content: His bone marrow stopped working, so no new white cells were made.
options.rationale: The count returned to normal, not to zero.

options.content: The bacteria killed many of his white blood cells, so the count fell.
options.rationale: He recovered, so the white cells won.

options.content: White blood cells turned into red blood cells.
options.rationale: White cells do not turn into red cells.

explanation: Increase $= 18\,000 - 7000 = 11\,000$ per mm³, which is $\dfrac{11\,000}{7000} \times 100 = 157\%$. More white cells were made to fight the infection: phagocytes engulfed and digested bacteria and lymphocytes made antibodies. Once the bacteria were cleared, the count returned to normal.
hints: Percentage increase = increase ÷ starting value × 100.
Name both types of white blood cell and what each does.
